title: A Student Posted His Answer Sheet Online. It Wasn't His Handwriting. India's Largest Exam Board Is Now in Crisis.
excerpt: CBSE's on-screen marking system swapped answer sheets, exposed student data through security flaws, and survived coordinated cyber attacks — all within weeks of launch. Parliament has stepped in.
body:
When Vedant Shrivastava, a Class 12 student in Delhi, opened the scanned copy of his Physics answer sheet, the handwriting was not his. The spacing was wrong. The answers were someone else's. He posted the evidence on X, and within hours, CBSE's new on-screen marking system — the one that was supposed to make grading more efficient — had become a national scandal.

CBSE acknowledged the error, sent the correct answer sheet, and promised to fix the result. But Vedant's case was not an isolated glitch. It was the first crack in a system that, over the following weeks, would face revelations of mass answer-sheet swaps, exposed student data, coordinated cyber attacks, and a parliamentary inquiry — all within the first month of the system's existence.

## How the System Broke

The on-screen marking system, or OSM, was introduced for the 2026 Class 12 board examinations. Physical answer sheets were scanned and uploaded online for teachers to grade digitally, replacing the older manual process where evaluators handled papers and totalled marks by hand. On paper, the upgrade promised fewer arithmetic errors and faster results.

What it delivered was something else. Students discovered pages so badly scanned they were illegible — yet evaluators had marked them with ticks and assigned scores. Some students received answer sheets that belonged to other candidates entirely. CBSE later admitted it had "discarded around 30 answer sheets due to issues like unclear images and duplicate entries" without re-scanning them, meaning some students may have been evaluated on nothing at all. Over four lakh students requested answer-sheet reviews.

## The Security Flaws

Then came the second wave. Sarthak Siddhant, an 18-year-old student, dug into CBSE's tender documents and found that the software provider, CoEmpt Eduteck — formerly known as Globarena Technologies — had been involved in the 2019 Telangana intermediate results controversy, where evaluation errors led to over 3.8 lakh students failing and 21 suicides. He appeared before a parliamentary committee to present his findings.

Days later, Nisarga Adhikary, a 19-year-old ethical hacker and CBSE student from Bengaluru, disclosed serious security flaws in the OSM portal. He had reported them to the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team in February 2026, but most remained unfixed. Adhikary alleged that attackers could access examiner accounts using publicly available details and a password embedded in the system's source code. He further claimed that answer sheets and question papers stored on an Amazon Web Services server were publicly accessible due to improper configuration.

On June 6, CBSE disclosed that its portal had been hit by "repeated and coordinated cyber attacks over the past three days," involving malicious traffic from IP addresses both within and outside India. The board filed a complaint with the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations unit of Delhi Police but maintained that no data breach had occurred.

## Parliament and the New Chairman

The crisis moved fast enough to reach Parliament. A standing committee summoned CBSE officials. The Education Ministry appointed a one-member committee to examine the board's procurement process for the OSM system. And in a move that signalled the scale of the fallout, CBSE received a new chairman and secretary — a leadership change that came in the middle of the firestorm.

The ruling party and the opposition traded accusations about responsibility. The Leader of Opposition demanded a probe into the contract allocation and called for the Education Minister's resignation. The ruling party accused opposition-led state governments of having used the same firm.

## Why NRI Families Are Watching

For the Indian diaspora, CBSE is not abstract. Hundreds of thousands of NRI families — particularly those who plan to send their children to India for higher education or whose relatives' children sit for board exams — rely on CBSE results as a foundational credential. The board conducts exams for over 40 lakh students annually.

The scandal has shaken a basic assumption: that the answer sheet marked by an examiner is, at minimum, the student's own work. Four teenagers — Vedant, Sarthak, Nisarga, and Rylen Anil, a 16-year-old who found vulnerabilities in the National Testing Agency's portal — used social media and basic technical tools to expose gaps that CBSE spent hundreds of crores building. As Forbes India noted, "Technology is a great leveller: a student sitting at home can scrutinise one of the country's largest education boards."

The question now is whether CBSE can rebuild trust before the next exam cycle begins. For millions of families, the answer cannot wait.

*Sources: Forbes India, Wikipedia (CBSE OSM controversy), Careers360, The Probe, CurrentIndia*
